You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say in Draconic, just above the trickle of the water, "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long breath there is only the water. Then a small voice answers from the dark, hoarse and sharp. "Who did Father leave to count the lambs the morning you fell?"

Your throat closes. "Nobody. I fell because I was counting them myself, and he carried me down one-handed and said I'd counted the same lamb twice."

A figure steps out of the black. She is smaller than you ever pictured, hood up, wiry, with a burn-scarred left hand and your father's jaw under the shadow. She looks you over, boots to horns, and her mouth starts to shake. Then she crosses the rocks in three steps and hits you like a thrown stone, arms locked round your ribs, and says into your chest, "You loud idiot. You came loud, you came so loud. I heard you singing from the wash-line."

You hold her. For a while neither of you says anything. When she lets go she wipes her face with the scarred hand, unembarrassed, and her voice goes quick and low.

She hid in the rocks above the Throat the night of the raid and lived on seeps and snared birds. The Foreman's scouts took her the winter after and kept her, because she could read and mend bindings. For years she has slept in the ledger-house at the third gate, reading what the Foreman writes. "Gorrak's bargain at the Border Stones is in the book. The Foreman never meant to let it stand. At midwinter's eve he sends riders to take the children back, and to take you, with your oath, for a second year. I've seen the page." She grips your wrist. "There's a key on his belt for the ledger chest. The page is the proof. With it, Gorrak's own people would turn on him. I can't take it alone. The midwinter feast is in four nights, and he'll be drunk, which is the only time he is."

Behind her, down the culvert, the water keeps running. Above, the wall torches gutter, and you have perhaps a quarter of an hour before the bell and Pip's cap.

Tessa is alive. She stands in front of you at the culvert, and the notebook and clock are now caught up with that scene. It is about 10:33 PM on day sixteen, and her quarter hour is running. What does Korvash say?

Your boots go back on, and you wade out onto the flat rocks. At the mouth of the arch you stop with your hands open and the handaxe still in your belt. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say in Draconic, just over the trickle of the water, "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long moment there is only the water. Then a voice answers from the dark, low and hoarse, a woman's voice with a girl's catch in it. "Say what I cut into your boots."

"A crescent with a bite out of it," you say. "The winter you were six. I wore them to the ground and you cried when I threw them out."

A shape unfolds from the black of the culvert, small for a dragonborn and wiry as rope, in a hooded grey mender's smock. She pushes the hood back. Her scales are the dark russet of old embers, dulled with soot. A pale scar runs through one brow, and one horn is broken short. She is twenty, and she has your father's jaw exactly as Veshra has. Her eyes are wet and furious and very bright.

She does not throw herself at you. She crosses the rocks in three quick steps, grips your forearms hard enough to hurt, and looks at your face as if checking it against a memory. Then her forehead drops against your chest, and her whole body shakes once, silently.

"You're so loud," she whispers into your tunic. "I heard you from the cairn. I heard you from the *road*."

She lets go and wipes her face with her wrist, an exact copy of your own gesture. Then the practical girl comes back into her eyes, and she glances up at the wall. "We've a quarter hour before the wall-walk changes. Listen. The Foreman keeps a ledger in the ledger-house, every hand he owes and every hand he's had, with the Tallies' names beside them. I've been mending its bindings since autumn so I could read it." Her voice drops. "Your name is in it. It was entered *before* the ford, Kor. Before you ever swore. Someone told him you were coming, and I think I know who, but I need you to hear the rest before you do anything loud."

The water runs over the stones. High above, a drunk laugh echoes along the wall.

It is half past ten on the night of day sixteen, with four days to midwinter's eve. What does Korvash say?

time: 30 minutes later: Day 16, 10:58:36 PM

You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call and speak into the dark in Draconic. The water trickles. Nothing answers.

Then a voice comes from the tunnel, close and low, hoarse from disuse. "Name the seventh goat."

Your throat locks. You were nine, and she was five, and the goat was the one that always came home last. "Ember," you say. "The one with the burnt-colored ear. You cried when she was sold."

A pause. Then a small figure steps out of the black onto the rocks, hood back. She is thin as a rope and wind-burnt, her scales a duller red than yours, a notch in one horn where something once struck it. She looks at you for a long moment, the way you looked at the goat on the stone. Then she crosses the rocks in three quick strides and hits you in the chest with both fists, hard, and holds on.

Neither of you says anything for some time.

When she steps back, her eyes are wet but her voice is steady. "You're loud," she says. "I could hear you from the wash-house." Then, quickly, the practical girl the rocks made: "We have a few minutes. Listen. I didn't hide in the Ledge forever. I came here at the autumn tally on purpose. The Foreman keeps a ledger of every hand the Tallies send him, and the village folk taken the night of the raid are in it, where they went, who's still alive. Other clan, Kor. Not just me."

She glances up toward the wall. "On midwinter's eve he holds the tally-feast. The stair thins to two guards, and every sergeant in the place will be at the tables. I can reach the ledger-house, but I can't get the book out past the gate-watch, and I can't do it quietly. I need something loud, somewhere else, at the right hour." The corner of her mouth lifts. "I thought of you."

She does not mention Gorrak, and when you start to, her face hardens. "He let me live. I haven't decided yet what that makes him."

Somewhere up the slope, a door bangs and a torch moves. It is nearly eleven. Midwinter's eve is four days off.

time: 25 minutes later: Day 16, 10:53:36 PM

You pull your boots on, wade out onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. Low and steady you hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say in Draconic, barely above the trickle: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long breath there is only the water. Then a small sound, a boot on wet stone, and a hooded figure steps out of the black, slim and wary, a dull iron needle held low in one hand like a knife. She stops three paces off. Her scales are the dark red of banked coals, her snout narrower than yours, and a thin white scar runs from one eye-ridge to her jaw. She looks at your horn charm, at the sash-less haft you aren't carrying, at your face.

"You're loud even when you're quiet," Tessa says. Her voice cracks on the last word. She laughs once, brokenly, and then she crosses the three paces and hits you in the chest with both fists, hard, and holds on. You put your arms around her and feel how thin she is, how she shakes. Neither of you says anything for a while.

When she pulls back, she scrubs her face with a sleeve. Her words come fast and low. She hid in the rocks the night of the raid and lived on what the high herders left out. She has been looking for the children taken from the clan ever since. The ledger-house at the third gate keeps the Foreman's book of "hands," every name he has ever bought or been sent, and she came in at the autumn tally as a mender to read it. She has. "Some of ours are alive, Kor. Taken fourteen years ago and put to the galleries. They're in the ledger by name. I can't carry them out. I can only carry the page."

She grips your wrist. "Midwinter's eve. Gorrak brings his tally to the Foreman and the third-gate guards will be at the count. I need something loud at the lower stair, loud enough to pull the stair guard down. You're good at that."

Her hood has slipped back. She is sixteen, maybe seventeen, and she has your father's jaw. It is nearly eleven at night. Four days remain until the eve, and the culvert wall above you is not as quiet as it was.

entries.text: notebook: updated Find Tessa
time: 40 minutes later: Day 16, 11:08:36 PM

You pull your boots on, wade out onto the flat rocks, and stop at the arch with your hands open. Low and steady you hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say in Draconic, just above the trickle of water: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long moment there is only the water. Then a voice comes out of the dark, flat and wary, a woman's voice with a girl's hoarseness still in it. "Say what you cut into my boot the winter I was six."

Your throat closes. "You cut it into mine," you say. "The crescent. You said it was so the goats would know whose feet to follow."

A small figure steps into the arch's mouth. She is slight and grey-green, hooded, with a mender's needle-case at her belt and a knife held low and ready. She lowers the hood. Your father's jaw looks out at you, and your mother's eyes. She is twenty, and she is seven years old, and she is also a stranger. She doesn't run to you. She looks you over, boots to horns, and only when she sees the sash on your belt does her knife hand shake.

"You're loud even when you're quiet," Tessa says, and then she is against your chest and you are holding her hard enough to hurt, both of you shaking, the water running on and on beside your boots.

Time is short, and she knows it first. She pulls back and speaks fast and low. Dargan hid her in the Weeping Ledge the night of the raid and told her not to come out until the horns stopped. She was in there three days. An old goat-woman hermit fed her afterward, and she has lived in the rocks since, until the autumn tally took a dozen herders from the steadings below and she walked in among them and let herself be counted. "The Foreman keeps a ledger of every hand he's been sent, with names and steadings. Every child Gorrak ever sold him, every herder, all of us. It's in the ledger-house on the third gate. If it's read out on midwinter's eve the way he always does, and if I can get it into the right hands, people will know where to look for all of them. I can reach the ledger. I can't carry it out alone."

Her eyes hold yours. "And Kor. Gorrak spared me at the Throat. I know. I'll thank him for it one day. But he has been feeding this place for fourteen years, so don't tell him a word of this."

The night bell tolls once, far above. She has to be back before the dawn count. "Dusk bell, day eighteen, here. Bring a plan, and bring your axe."

She pulls her hood up and is gone into the tunnel, light as a goat on rock. It is a little past eleven at night, on day sixteen, with four days until midwinter's eve.

She tested Korvash with a question only he could answer (the boots she scratched the crescent on). She has been inside Greyshaft since the autumn tally, working as a mender to reach the ledger-house, where the Foreman keeps the 'hands' ledger. She reveals the ledger lists names of every stolen child and laborer, plus a book of debts that binds hobgoblin captains like Gorrak. entries.text: notebook: updated Find Tessa
time: 15 minutes later: Day 16, 10:43:36 PM

You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. The three notes of Dargan's call go out low into the dark, and the water goes on trickling after them. Then you say it in Draconic: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

Nothing, for ten heartbeats. Then a pebble clicks deep in the tunnel, and a small hooded figure steps into the thin light at the arch's mouth, a body's length from you, with a mending knife held low and ready in her left hand.

"Say what I did to your boots," she says. Her voice is rough and quiet and grown. It is still hers.

"The winter you were six, you cut a crescent into the left heel with Father's awl," you say. "I wore it two years. Mother said it would bring me luck, and I never took it off the heel."

The knife drops. She pushes the hood back. She is small and wiry and weathered, with Dargan's jaw, a crescent-shaped scar across the back of her left hand, and eyes you would know in a crowd of thousands. She doesn't run at you. She stands very straight, shaking, and says, "You're so *loud*. I heard you from the Throat. Everyone did." Her face breaks, and then she is against your chest, and your arms close around her, and the sluice runs over the stones as if nothing had changed.

When she can speak, she says it fast and low, with one eye on the arch. She lived in the rocks after the raid, fed by goats and by strangers, and learned the hobgoblins' ways from a hundred ridges. Two seasons ago she heard what the Tallies were selling, and to whom, and followed it here. She has mended the Foreman's ledger-bindings since the autumn tally, and what she's seen in them makes her hands go cold. "Every name, Kor. Every child, every laborer, with the steading and the price. And a second book, the debts. Every captain who owes the Foreman a quota, with the sum. Gorrak's page is thick. That book is what holds them all to him. Without it they're just raiders. With it, they're his."

She grips your sleeve. "The quota-caravan leaves on midwinter's eve, four days from now, with everything in those books going out on it. After that I can't reach them. I need the ledger, and I need an axe to get me up the stair. I've been waiting for you."

It is a little before eleven at night. Above you the drunk pair are laughing on the wall, and the third gate's stair has six sworn hobgoblins and a hundred steps. What does Korvash say?

time: 5 minutes later: Day 16, 10:33:36 PM

You pull on your boots, wade out onto the flat rocks, and stop under the arch with your hands open and the handaxe still in your belt. The water talks quietly around your ankles. You hum the first three notes of your father's evening call, low and steady, and say in Draconic, just above the trickle: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

Nothing moves. Then a pebble clicks somewhere deep in the dark, and a voice answers, rough and quiet, a woman's voice in the old tongue. "Say the seventh goat."

You do not have to think. "She comes home by the north fold, because she's too stubborn to use the gate."

A pause, long as a held breath. Then a small figure steps out of the black, hood up, a short knife held low in one hand, point down. She is shorter than you by a head and lean as a rope. When she pushes the hood back, you see red scales dulled by soot and a notch bitten out of one frill, and her father's jaw. Her hands are scarred across the fingers by years of needle and tin. Her eyes are Dargan's.

She does not run to you. She stares, and you see her measure the horn charm, the sash, the axe-calluses, and the width of you, as if checking a count. "You got big," she says at last, flat, and her voice cracks right down the middle of it. The knife drops to her side. "I wasn't sure you'd come. I wasn't sure you'd *know* me."

Water drips from the arch. Above you the wall torches flicker, and somewhere a drunk guard laughs. She glances up once, quick as a goat, then back to you.

"We haven't got long," she says, "and I've waited fourteen years to say this, so listen before you break something. I don't need to be carried out of here. There's a ledger in that house with the name of every child this place has ever taken, and I have been copying it a page at a time. I need you to help me finish."

It is half past ten at night. What does Korvash do?

You pull your boots on, wade out onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. The three notes of your father's evening call go into the dark, low and a little cracked. Then, in Draconic: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

The water trickles. Nothing answers for a long moment. Then a voice comes out of the black, thin and level, much older than the six-year-old you remember.

"Say the name of the goat. The one Dargan named for his mother."

You have not thought of that goat in years. It was the old brown nanny with the torn ear, who butted you off the fold wall every spring. "Grumble-Aunt," you say, and your voice goes rough on it. "Grumble-Aunt. You used to hide in her straw so Father wouldn't find you at bedtime."

A small figure steps out of the culvert's shadow, hood up, a bundle of wet cloths under one arm. She stops three paces off, just beyond the reach of your arm, as if she has learned exactly how far that is. When she pushes the hood back, the face under it is thin and sharp, with Dargan's jaw and your mother's eyes, and a scar through one eyebrow you never gave her. Her scales are dull red, a shade paler than yours, and ash-streaked.

She does not run to you. She looks you over from boots to horns, and her mouth works once. "You're loud," she says, in Draconic, almost a whisper. "I heard you from the third gate. You were never any good at quiet." Then her composure cracks all at once, and she crosses the three paces and hits you in the chest with both fists, hard, and then holds on.

She is shaking. When she speaks again it is rapid and low, into your tunic. "I haven't got long. The mender's bell rings at eleven, and the ledger-house stair is counted. Listen. The Foreman isn't what Gorrak thinks. He's not only short of hands. He keeps a second ledger, and your name's in it, Kor. Not as an axe." She pulls back and looks up at you. "I've seen the page."

Above you on the wall, the torch moves. It is half past ten. You have, at most, a few minutes. What does Korvash say?

You went down on the rubble heap with the shield still up and the bellow still in your throat. The arrow caught you above the rim and the world went out like a snuffed lamp.

You come back to it slowly. The first thing you know is the cold, and the second is rope biting your wrists behind you. You are propped against a boulder on the lip of the gully with your boots lashed together. The sun is well up and it must be nearly ten. Your side and shoulder burn, but you are breathing, and that is more than you counted on.

The sword, the shield and Hask's key ring are gone. The scout archer sits a few paces off with his bow across his knees, chewing a strip of something and watching you without malice. The other scout is nowhere in sight. When your eyes find the empty place beside him, the archer says in flat Common, "Gone to tell the Foreman you're alive. He'll want you in one piece. He says so every time."

You look down the gully. The track is empty to the first bend. No column, no small figures on the scree, no rust-red hood. The slate you pulled half-down lies where it fell, and past it there is only wind. Three hours is a long head start for children who have been told not to stop.

Whether Tessa carried them to safety or whether the Foreman's riders are already among them, you cannot tell from here. You have one hit point and no weapon. One man with a bow watches you, and soon the other will be back with more.

You set the boy down. "Run to Tessa, lad, and don't stop." Then you climb the rubble heap with the shield up and the sword out. You bellow up the gully in Goblin and Common alike, as loud as your cracked voice will go. It comes out ragged. You are one wounded dragonborn on a heap of slate, and the scouts on the ridge can see it.

Neither of them answers. The archer simply draws.

His first arrow is fast and low, and it comes in over the shield's rim. It hits you at the base of the throat. You feel the blow before you feel the pain. His second arrow goes wide and skitters away down the slate. The first was enough.

Your knees go. The sword slips from your hand and the shield drags your arm down. The gully tilts and the grey sky turns over. You hear Ninna still counting below you, steady and unbroken, and the small boy's running feet. Far ahead, a rust-red figure turns on the track and starts back toward you. She is too far away to reach you.

You don't hear the end of the count. You hear Tessa's voice, once, calling your name in Draconic. Then the sound of the gully thins away and goes quiet.

Korvash Emberhide dies on the slate at the Greyshaft gully, shortly before seven in the morning on the nineteenth day. His last act was to stand between ninety-four children and the men hunting them. By the rules, the arrow that finished him was a critical hit, and the damage was more than your maximum hit points even after what was already gone. At 2 hit points, there was no chance to make a death saving throw.

That is the end of Korvash's story. I'm sorry. He went out the way he lived, loud and in front. If you'd like, I can build a new character who picks up the aftermath: Tessa, Ninna and the children on the goat track, the Foreman's ledger still unburned, and Gorrak Vael's oath with no axe left to hold it. Or we can start a different adventure entirely. Which would you like?

Two grey-cloaked scouts stand by the door, one rubbing a bowstring with wax. Between you and the desk, a heavy man in a leather apron sits on a stool, turning brass tallying beads one at a time through his fingers. He does not look up.

time: 2 minutes later: Day 19, 6:52:12 AM

You set the boy down and he goes pelting up the track toward Tessa's red scales. Then you climb the rubble heap with the shield up and the sword out. You are one battered dragonborn with a cracked voice, and you pitch it so it rolls up the gully like a rockfall, Goblin first, then Common. Your own name comes out last.

It works better than it has any right to. The archer's string eases. The swordsman's weight shifts back onto his heels. They are scouts, not wall-breakers, and they have just heard that you are "a whole camp's worth of me" with your father's name for a battle-cry. Neither of them knows that you are two hit points from the ground.

For a long breath nobody moves. Then the swordsman says something short to the archer. The archer lowers his bow and slides back off the lip of the ridge, running low toward Greyshaft with the news. The swordsman stays. He keeps to the skyline, a grey shape thirty feet up and always the same distance behind, watching every child and not coming any closer.

He will not attack alone while you stand here, but he is counting you, and the Foreman will have your name before the morning bell finishes. The column is moving. Tessa and Ninna are at the head, and the last of the children are crossing the gully floor toward the stream.

It is a few minutes before seven in the morning. You are at 2 hit points with a shadow on the ridge and an open road. What does Korvash do?

sheet.name: Korvash Emberhide
sheet.opening: Korvash Emberhide, a hulking red-scaled dragonborn barbarian (Chaotic Good, loud, proud, quick to anger; ideal Charity; bond: he keeps his word no matter what; flaw: inflexible), arrives at dusk in a lowland market town near the foot of the mountains, driving off a pack of bullies shaking down a family of herders, as he has done for years. His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. Hook for the opening: just after the bullies flee, a frightened young herder or a traveler brings him word, perhaps carried from Aunt Veshra, that a hobgoblin warband bearing a tin-masked captain and a notched rod has been seen again, or that something connected to the Goat's Throat has turned up. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. Invent only original places and people; keep it grounded in the SRD's monsters (hobgoblins, goblins, bugbears, wolves, etc.).
